cards.title: How the brains work
cards.text: How heroes and enemies decide what to do today, in five parts. Mark any part that's off.
cards.why: This is built the way you asked. The questions after it are about what's missing.

parts.title: Picking a target
parts.text: Nearest first, plus a nudge each: archer likes hurt enemies it can see, rogue likes hurt or distracted ones, knight likes enemies attacking a teammate, rats like the archer. They stick with a target a while.

parts.title: Choosing how to move
parts.text: Approach, hold, kite, strafe, flank, retreat or wander, re-scored every 0.4s. The best usually wins, but by chance, with a bonus for the current one and a minimum time before switching.

parts.title: Steering
parts.text: Each unit scores 16 directions: wanting to go towards its goal, avoiding walls, pillars, hazards and crowding teammates. It moves the best way. No flow fields.

parts.title: Abilities
parts.text: Checked every half second. Better moments give better odds: Barrage on groups, Charge through a line, Shadow Step on a distracted target. Odds jump when one enemy is left.

parts.title: Pathfinding
parts.text: None. Steering only looks about two body widths ahead, which is fine in open rooms with round pillars.

cards.title: Pathfinding
cards.text: Steering alone gets stuck in dead ends once rooms have walls. How should units find their way?
cards.why: Needed before rooms get shapes. Without it, a hero behind a wall walks into it forever instead of going round.
cards.pick: A route through corner points around walls, worked out when the target moves. The next point becomes a 'go here' for the steering.
cards.details:
This keeps your context steering as the part that moves units; the route only tells it where to head next. It's not a flow field: each unit gets its own short route, only when it can't see its target.

In open rooms nothing changes, since a unit that can see its target goes straight for it as now.

cards.title: The rogue keeps dying
cards.text: The rogue is downed most often and ends up the lowest level. Fix the brain or the numbers?
cards.why: A hero who keeps falling behind stops being fun to bring.
cards.pick: The brain first: when hurt, retreat behind the knight and skip backstabs. Only raise HP if that's not enough.
cards.details: Why it happens: Shadow Step teleports the rogue behind enemies, often into the middle of a pack, and it keeps darting in at low HP.

cards.title: Party teamwork
cards.text: Each hero picks targets by itself. Which bit of teamwork should go in first?
cards.why: Small team habits make the party look like it's working together, which is most of what you watch.

options.label: Knight draws attention
options.text: Enemies he hits or charges go for him for a few seconds.

options.label: Finish the kill
options.text: Archer and rogue prefer a nearly dead enemy.

options.label: Knight protects
options.text: He goes to whoever is low and being attacked.

options.label: Walking formation
options.text: Knight in front, archer behind, between fights.

cards.title: Enemy habits
cards.text: Enemies use the same brain as heroes with different numbers. Should each type get a habit of its own?
cards.why: You can tell enemies apart by how they move, not just by how they look, and each one asks something different of your party.
cards.pick: Yes: rats scatter when only one or two are left, skeletons line up shoulder to shoulder, the boss goes for whoever is alone.
cards.details: Slimes already split when they die, so they have their thing.

cards.title: Knowing about combos
cards.text: Should the brains know about status combos, like luring enemies into oil before using fire?
cards.why: It's the difference between combos happening by luck and heroes visibly setting them up, which is the most fun to watch.
cards.pick: A little: the knight prefers to Charge enemies towards hazards, and Barrage prefers targets standing in oil or gas.
